article_title: Code as Anchor, Memory and Metaphor as Support: Learner Experiences with Multi-View Visualizations
citation: Naaz Sibia, Jessica Wen, Amber Richardson, Yashika Jain, Khushi Malik, Bogdan Simion, Carolina Nobre, Angela Zavaleta Bernuy, Andrew Petersen, and Michael Liut. 2026. Code as Anchor, Memory and Metaphor as Support: Learner Experiences with Multi-View Visualizations. ICER 2026 Vol. 1. https://doi.org/10.1145/3765964.3811662
title: Multi-representational program visualization tool with synchronized code, memory, and metaphor views
description: A web-based visualization probe designed for the study, drawing on MER/DeFT and concreteness fading. The article states the authors "designed a visualization tool with multiple views that draws on MER/DeFT and concreteness fading to address limitations of existing program visualization tools." Its interface presents three synchronized panes — Code View with the active line highlighted, Memory View aligned with Python Tutor's representation, and Metaphor View using analogy-based depictions (house for scope, magician's table for while loops, relay race for linked lists) — with brushing and linking across views and step controls. It was refined across three formative feedback cycles with instructors, a visualization researcher, and nine teaching assistants.
requirements: Formative refinement for conceptual fidelity, usability, and alignment with common student misconceptions; synchronized execution across views
constraints: The CS2 configuration steps through execution at function level rather than line by line, which participants criticized as undermining the tool's purpose
target_learners: undergraduate students who have completed CS1 and CS2
target_learning_goals: tracing, explaining, and extending code across scope, while loops, and linked lists
examples: All visualization materials are openly available at the authors' GitHub repository, and reproducible gaze analysis code is available on OSF
key_sources: Naaz Sibia, Jessica Wen, Amber Richardson, Yashika Jain, Khushi Malik, Bogdan Simion, Carolina Nobre, Angela Zavaleta Bernuy, Andrew Petersen, and Michael Liut. 2026. Code as Anchor, Memory and Metaphor as Support: Learner Experiences with Multi-View Visualizations. ICER 2026 Vol. 1. https://doi.org/10.1145/3765964.3811662

citation: Gerry Stahl & Friedrich Hesse. (2010). A prism of CSCL research. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-010-9087-3
title: Mr. Vetro simulation framework for collaborative exploration of the cardiovascular system
description: Mr. Vetro is a student-facing simulation of the human body's cardiovascular system of lungs and heart, built on a substantial extension of the Agentsheets student-programmable simulation design environment. The editorial states that "the Mr. Vetro simulation framework allows students to explore the effects of different variations of physiological parameters within an interdependent complex system." Students collaboratively control the simulation, each simulating an individual organ or contextual parameter through mobile devices, in an approach the authors call collective simulations.
requirements: Small groups of students, each with a mobile device, simulating individual organs or contextual parameters
constraints: The medium is necessarily simplified, implemented in computer graphics, per the editorial's discussion of representing complex scientific phenomena
target_learning_goals: Principles of human anatomy and physiology
examples: Students interact to collaboratively control the simulation of a complex organism under varying conditions by each simulating the role of individual organs or contextual parameters through mobile devices
key_sources: Gerry Stahl & Friedrich Hesse. (2010). A prism of CSCL research. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-010-9087-3

article_title: Significance of forms and foci of metacognitive regulation in collaborative science learning of less and more successful outcome groups in diverse contexts
citation: Iiskala, T., Volet, S., Jones, C., Koretsky, M., & Vauras, M. (2021). Significance of forms and foci of metacognitive regulation in collaborative science learning of less and more successful outcome groups in diverse contexts. Instructional Science, 49, 687–718. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-021-09558-1
title: Forms and foci framework of metacognitive regulation in collaborative learning
description: A conceptual framework for describing metacognitive regulation (MR) in collaborative learning along two axes: forms (whose cognitive process is regulated and how the group is involved) and foci (the level of cognitive activity being regulated). Forms include VMSR ("observable evidence of a group member's MR of their own learning despite the joint effort"), IMR (a member attempting to regulate the group but being ignored), MOR ("asymmetric metacognitive interaction between partners"), and SSMR (several members' interdependent regulation of joint cognitive activity). Foci distinguish high-level (elaboration, constructing meaning) from low-level (simple acquisition, practical task aspects) cognitive activity. The article uses this framework to examine outcomes across three diverse contexts.
requirements: A shared group goal, since "the manifestation of social forms of MR, especially SSMR, presupposes the existence of a group's common goal."
constraints: Only verbalised MR is observable; most self-regulation is assumed internal and "not accessible to peers or researchers."
key_sources: Iiskala, T., Volet, S., Jones, C., Koretsky, M., & Vauras, M. (2021). Significance of forms and foci of metacognitive regulation in collaborative science learning of less and more successful outcome groups in diverse contexts. Instructional Science, 49, 687–718. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-021-09558-1

article_title: Development and validation of a scale for metacognitive regulation of interactive metadiscourse strategies in L2 argumentative writing
citation: Chenghui Chen, Lawrence Jun Zhang. (2025). Development and validation of a scale for metacognitive regulation of interactive metadiscourse strategies in L2 argumentative writing. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-025-09435-z
title: MRIM scale: a 19-item instrument for metacognitive regulation of interactive metadiscourse strategies in L2 argumentative writing
description: The MRIM scale is a 6-point Likert questionnaire measuring L2 learners' metacognitive regulation of interactive metadiscourse in argumentative writing. Items were generated through literature review and unstructured interviews with nine students, then piloted with PhD reviewers, two content experts, and a 117-student pretest. The finalized 19-item scale comprises three subscales: planning of interactive metadiscourse (PIM), monitoring of interactive metadiscourse (MIM), and evaluating of interactive metadiscourse (EIM).
requirements: Items were generated through literature review and unstructured interviews with target participants, which the authors say can increase the credibility and quality of items
constraints: The scale was developed and validated with first-year non-English major students at two Chinese universities, so its validated scope is that population
target_learners: first-year non-English major university students learning English as a foreign language
target_learning_goals: metacognitive regulation of interactive metadiscourse strategies in L2 argumentative writing
examples: Sample One (1417 cases) completed the original version for EFA; Sample Two (1078 cases) wrote a timed argumentative essay and completed the revised version for CFA and regression
key_sources: Chenghui Chen, Lawrence Jun Zhang. (2025). Development and validation of a scale for metacognitive regulation of interactive metadiscourse strategies in L2 argumentative writing. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-025-09435-z

article_title: Metacognitive regulation in physical therapists' clinical reasoning: a scoping review.
citation: Perdrix Yannick, Nael Jérémy, Dionne Eric, Pinsault Nicolas. (2026). Metacognitive regulation in physical therapists’ clinical reasoning: a scoping review. International Journal of Medical Education. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC13563282/
title: Existing assessment methods for MR in PT clinical reasoning: qualitative scored reflections and quantitative calibration/certainty measurement
description: The review identified only four studies assessing MR in PT clinical reasoning, organized into two categories. Qualitative-data-based assessments score student data from placement situations (peer blogging, a critical reflection assessment task marked out of 100, a guided personal reflective report worth 20% of the placement mark). One study quantifies MR by measuring calibration — "the correlation between performance judgment and actual performance" — and certainty, defined as "a subjective estimate of expected performance", via prediction and postdiction sections on assignments. The article concludes that "the proposals remain much more limited than for other professions" and none reported a qualitative or psychometric evaluation of their method.
requirements: Assessment must be task-dependent; five self-questionnaire-based articles were excluded on this ground
constraints: None of the four studies reported a qualitative or psychometric evaluation; communication was not specifically addressed by any method
target_learners: Physical therapy students on clinical placements
examples: The critical reflection assessment task based on placement situations, marked out of 100 with subjective markers
key_sources: Perdrix Yannick, Nael Jérémy, Dionne Eric, Pinsault Nicolas. (2026). Metacognitive regulation in physical therapists’ clinical reasoning: a scoping review. International Journal of Medical Education. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC13563282/

article_title: Simulation training significantly improves the performance of novice students achieving the standard transesophageal echocardiography views.
citation: Siniarski Aleksander, Piątek Paweł, Karcińska Aleksandra, del Carmen Yika Alicia, Szostek Kamil, Dziwiński Tomasz, Stąpór Maciej, Golińska-Grzybała Karolina, Piórkowski Adam, Gackowski Andrzej. (2025). Simulation training significantly improves the performance of novice students achieving the standard transesophageal echocardiography views. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-06917-1
title: MrTEEmothy TEE simulator with EduTool automated guidance for standardized TEE view training
description: The MrTEEmothy simulator (Medical Simulation Technologies, Krakow) comprises a phantom, a laptop, and a generic TEE probe whose depth, rotation, bends and plane angle are sensed and logged continuously. Its "EduTool" deployed "well-established echocardiographic projections that adhere to the prevailing guidelines set by the ASE", providing automated guidance on requisite probe movements in a predetermined sequence and logging precision, time, and per-sensor motion time series for retrospective analysis.
requirements: Requires the simulator hardware (phantom, laptop, TEE probe) and tailored presets aligned to the research protocol; students first receive a didactic video lecture and initial 45 min training to acquaint themselves with probe movements.
constraints: Only results from this specific simulator were compared, so outcomes may vary by simulator type/brand; the simulator remains an artificial device, raising questions about transfer of skills to real-life situations.
target_learners: Medical students with basic heart anatomy knowledge but no prior echocardiography training
Cardiovascular clinicians and residents learning TEE
target_learning_goals: Acquiring standard transesophageal echocardiography views with correct probe manipulation
Performing safe TEE examinations with minimal unnecessary probe movements
examples: Students received unrestricted access to recorded video lectures, an initial 45-minute familiarization session, then one to four weeks of unlimited simulator practice before Test 2.
key_sources: Siniarski Aleksander, Piątek Paweł, Karcińska Aleksandra, del Carmen Yika Alicia, Szostek Kamil, Dziwiński Tomasz, Stąpór Maciej, Golińska-Grzybała Karolina, Piórkowski Adam, Gackowski Andrzej. (2025). Simulation training significantly improves the performance of novice students achieving the standard transesophageal echocardiography views. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-06917-1

article_title: A mixed-reality stimulator for lumbar puncture training: a pilot study.
citation: Huang Xiaojing, Yan Zhaoxia, Gong Chao, Zhou Zheliang, Xu Hua, Qin Chunhui, Wang Zhenwei. (2023). A mixed-reality stimulator for lumbar puncture training: a pilot study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-023-04173-9
title: Mixed-reality lumbar puncture simulator using HoloLens glasses and 3D vertebral images overlaid on a standard mannequin.
description: A standard lumbar puncture mannequin without internal landmarks was augmented with 1:1-scaled 3D vertebral images generated from 0.625 mm CT scans and displayed via first-generation Microsoft HoloLens glasses, allowing trainees to see internal anatomical structures during needling practice. The MR technology was independently developed by Dr. Qin (Patent application No. CN201710414454 in China, 2019). Two independent anesthesiologists judged the simulator to be anatomically correct.
requirements: Standard lumbar puncture mannequin without internal landmarks
3D vertebral image models scaled 1:1 to the simulator
constraints: HoloLens glasses had a slight time delay in appearance
Helmet was too heavy, causing soreness in the shoulder and neck
Not very friendly to trainees who wear glasses
examples: Trainees located the L3-L4 interspace by palpation, then practiced needle insertion with internal 3D anatomy in view through glasses, then without it; correct insertion into the subarachnoid space was confirmed by fluid flowing out of the needle.
key_sources: Huang Xiaojing, Yan Zhaoxia, Gong Chao, Zhou Zheliang, Xu Hua, Qin Chunhui, Wang Zhenwei. (2023). A mixed-reality stimulator for lumbar puncture training: a pilot study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-023-04173-9
